text: Deep down, Captain Harlow knew the ice would never let them go. Night after night he lay awake in his bunk, thinking of his wife and daughter back home, a palpable sense of dread settling over him. The expedition had been trapped for ninety days.
strengths: the ninety days and the family at home are real stakes
weaknesses: claims to know what the captain knew deep down
invents his sleepless nights and his thoughts
tells the listener the mood instead of giving the facts that make it
the one hard fact arrives last
spokenRhythm: An interior claim, a long sentence of invented feeling, then the only fact in a short close.
narrativeFunction: Meant to make the captain sympathetic, but does it by putting thoughts in his head that no record supplies.
whyItFails: Nothing in a log or a letter tells us what a man knew deep down or how he slept, so two of the three sentences are fiction presented as history. Used on a real person, this puts feelings into someone who cannot answer for them. The palpable sense of dread is the narrator telling the listener what to feel, when ninety days in the ice and a family at home would do it without help.
rewrite: The expedition had been trapped in the ice for ninety days. Captain Harlow had a wife and a daughter at home.

text: Meet Josiah Crane. A visionary. A gambler. This former draper's clerk raised the equivalent of tens of millions in today's money for a forty-mile railway, and little did he know it would seal his destiny.
strengths: a draper's clerk raising money for a forty-mile railway is a real story in a few words
weaknesses: a game-show introduction followed by labels instead of deeds
an invented modern conversion presented as fact
a stock phrase and a word from a trailer in place of what happened to him
spokenRhythm: Three clipped fragments like a drumroll, then one overloaded sentence carrying the facts, a conversion and a tease.
narrativeFunction: Meant to introduce the promoter of a railway, but labels him before showing anything he did.
whyItFails: Visionary and gambler are verdicts the listener should reach from the evidence, and the fragment run turns the introduction into a trailer. The modern figure is a conversion no record supports, and it sounds precise while meaning nothing. Little did he know and destiny close on a micro-hook that promises a downfall without saying what it was, holding the story back to sound dramatic.
rewrite: Josiah Crane had been a draper's clerk. He raised the money for a forty-mile railway.

text: Who was Mary Tull? A simple innkeeper? A grieving widow? The truth is, Mary Tull was not just an innkeeper, but the woman who controlled every cask of salt that moved through the valley.
strengths: the salt casks are a strong, concrete measure of her power
weaknesses: three questions in a row before a single fact
the truth is announces a reveal instead of making one
not just X but Y frames her as a twist instead of a person
spokenRhythm: Three short questions in a row, then one long sentence that announces a reveal and delivers it in the same breath.
narrativeFunction: Meant to introduce a woman with unexpected power, but stages her introduction as a quiz.
whyItFails: The listener is asked questions the narrator answers at once, which is a quiz-show habit rather than a way of telling a story. The truth is and not just, but both announce that a surprise is coming, so the surprise is spent before it arrives. Introduced plainly by what she did, she would have been more surprising.
rewrite: Mary Tull kept an inn. She also controlled every cask of salt that moved through the valley.

text: Thomas Garrow, the harbourmaster, adjusts his spectacles and peers at the ledger, his weathered face lit by the oil lamp. He sighs — runs a finger down the column — and stops. Something is wrong. Two hundred barrels of whale oil are missing.
strengths: the missing barrels are a clear, countable fact
weaknesses: spectacles, lamp, sigh and finger are all the camera's job
a manufactured beat of suspense before the fact
spokenRhythm: A long descriptive sentence, a broken one full of dashes, a three-word beat, then the fact.
narrativeFunction: Meant to introduce the harbourmaster and the loss together, but spends its words acting out a scene.
whyItFails: It introduces a man by his face and his gestures, which the picture shows or the film has no evidence for, instead of by his job and what he found. The dashes make the narrator sound breathless, and the three-word beat tells the listener to be tense before giving them a reason. The fact that matters waits until the end.
rewrite: Thomas Garrow was the harbourmaster. According to the ledger, two hundred barrels of whale oil were missing.

text: Clara Voss wasn't just a physician. She was a force of nature. Remarkably, during the fever summer she treated more than three hundred patients in the river district, and her name would be remembered forever. But her greatest battle was yet to come.
strengths: three hundred patients in one summer is a real measure of her work
weaknesses: a contrast formula and a cliché in place of an introduction
a hype adverb tells the listener to be impressed
a claim about being remembered forever that nothing supports
ends on a tease instead of the next fact
spokenRhythm: Two short sentences of build-up, a long one that buries the fact between an adverb and a boast, and a teasing close.
narrativeFunction: Meant to introduce a physician by her achievement, but surrounds the achievement with praise.
whyItFails: The one thing she did, treating more than three hundred patients, would introduce her perfectly, and it is wrapped in a formula, a cliché and an adverb that tell the listener how to rate her. Remembered forever is trailer language, and the last line is a micro-hook that withholds the next part of the story to sound exciting.
rewrite: Clara Voss was a physician. During the fever summer, she treated more than three hundred patients in the river district.
